d: What Aurora OS is, what this documentation covers and how it is organized
x: Aurora OS is a desktop Linux distribution built on Debian 13 “trixie” . It runs its own desktop, written for Aurora in Python with GTK 4 and libadwaita, on the Wayfire Wayland compositor (with labwc as a compatibility session). It ships as a live ISO that you can try without installing and install with a graphical installer. # What this documentation covers Everything a user or administrator can see or change in Aurora OS: Getting started : requirements, the live USB, the boot menu, installation and the first boot. Sessions and login : the login screen, the two desktop sessions, what happens when a session starts, locking, idle and power. The desktop : the top bar, the Aurora menu, the Control Center, notifications, the dock, Spotlight, Launchpad, the overview, workspaces, hot corners, gestures, desktop icons and widgets. Windows : moving and resizing, snapping, Snap Layouts, Always on Top, animations. Apps : the apps written for Aurora (Files, Task Manager, Settings, Dev Hub, Game Hub, the Assistant) and the ones included. Settings reference : every page of Settings and every option on it. System : updates and restarts, snapshots, backups, storage, screen time, security, networking, sharing, devices, accessibility and languages. Aurora AI : the assistant, writing tools, dictation, read aloud and where answers come from. Virtual machines and Troubleshooting . Reference : keyboard shortcuts, shell commands, command-line tools, configuration files, GSettings keys, environment variables and file locations. The reference pages (shortcuts, settings keys, Settings options, widgets, catalogs) are generated from Aurora's source code each time this documentation is built, so they match the release you are reading about. # Conventions Super The key with the Windows logo (or ⌘ on Apple keyboards). Tapping it alone opens Spotlight. Settings → Page → Option A path in the Settings app. Open Settings with Super + I , from the Aurora menu or from the Control Center. monospace Commands to type in a terminal ( Super + Enter opens one), file names and settings keys. Compatibility session Something that only exists in the Aurora Compatibility (labwc) session. # Versions This documentation describes the latest Aurora OS release . Aurora follows Debian trixie for the base system and the Linux 6.12 LTS kernel; Aurora's own desktop is updated through the aurora-desktop and aurora-artwork packages. See Updates and restarts .

d: The hardware Aurora OS needs, and what works best
x: # Minimum and recommended Minimum Recommended Processor 64-bit x86 (amd64), 2 cores 4 cores or more Memory 2 GB (the installer checks this) 4 GB; 8 GB or more for Aurora AI models on the computer Disk 20 GB (the installer checks this) 64 GB or more, SSD Graphics Any; without 3D acceleration Aurora draws on the processor Intel, AMD or NVIDIA with a working Mesa or NVIDIA driver Firmware BIOS or UEFI UEFI USB stick 4 GB 8 GB, USB 3 # Hardware support Firmware for Intel, AMD, Realtek, Atheros, Broadcom and MediaTek Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, GPUs and audio (Sound Open Firmware). Mesa with Vulkan and VA-API video decoding, the Intel media driver; NVIDIA cards are detected and Settings → Software Updates → Additional Drivers installs the recommended proprietary driver. Laptops: power profiles, thermald, screen rotation, firmware updates (fwupd), backlight, battery health and an 80% charge limit where the firmware supports it. Fingerprint readers (fprintd), printers (CUPS, driverless IPP) and scanners. Virtual machines: QEMU/KVM (guest agent, SPICE), VirtualBox, VMware and Hyper-V guest tools are included. See Virtual machines . Secure Boot. The live USB's boot loader is not signed yet: turn Secure Boot off in the firmware settings to start it. An installed system on UEFI can use Secure Boot again (it boots through Debian's signed shim).

d: Download or build the ISO, check it, and write it to a USB stick
h: Write it to a USB stick
Try it without a USB stick
x: # The ISO Aurora OS is an image named aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso that boots on BIOS and UEFI computers. Download it from the website or build it yourself ( Building Aurora ). GitHub limits files to 2 GB, so a larger image is published in numbered parts. Download every part and join them first: cat aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso.part-* > aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso Then check the reconstructed image against its checksum file before writing it: sha256sum -c aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso.sha256 The output must say OK . If it doesn't, download the ISO again. # Write it to a USB stick Use a stick of 4 GB or more. Everything on it is erased. # On any system balenaEtcher or Fedora Media Writer : choose the ISO, choose the stick, write. Ventoy : copy the ISO onto a Ventoy stick like any file; Ventoy shows it in its menu. Rufus on Windows: choose DD image mode when it asks. # On Linux, from a terminal Find the stick's device name with lsblk (for example /dev/sdb ), then write the image. Check the name twice: writing to the wrong disk destroys its data. sudo dd if=aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync # Try it without a USB stick Boot the ISO in a virtual machine: QEMU, GNOME Boxes, virt-manager, VirtualBox, VMware or Hyper-V. See Virtual machines .

d: Every entry of the USB stick's boot menu, and the firmware's boot keys
x: # Starting from the USB stick Plug in the stick and restart the computer. Open the firmware's boot menu. The key depends on the maker: usually F12 , F10 , F9 , F11 , Esc or Del , pressed right after switching on. Choose the USB stick (on UEFI computers, the entry that starts with “UEFI”). # Entries Entry What it does Try Aurora OS Starts the live desktop in English. Nothing is written to the computer's disks. Install Aurora OS Starts the live system and opens the installer straight away. Try Aurora OS (safe graphics) For graphics cards that give a black screen: starts the Aurora Compatibility session with the plainest drawing path (adds aurora.safegraphics nouveau.noaccel=1 ). Language · Lingua · Sprache · Idioma A submenu with 20 languages. Each starts the live system in that language with the matching keyboard layout ( aurora.lang= and aurora.kbd= ). Boot from hard disk Skips the stick and starts what is installed on the computer. UEFI firmware settings On UEFI computers: reboots into the firmware setup (to change the boot order or Secure Boot). # Boot parameters Press E on an entry to edit its kernel line for one boot (press Ctrl + X or F10 to start). Useful additions: aurora.lang=it_IT.UTF-8 The live session's language. aurora.kbd=it The keyboard layout; several separated by commas ( us,ru ), switched with Alt + Shift . aurora.safegraphics Use the Compatibility session with software drawing. nomodeset Disables the kernel's graphics drivers: a last resort for a black screen. aurora.install Open the installer after the desktop starts (what “Install Aurora OS” adds).

d: Using Aurora from the USB stick before installing it
h: What is different from an installed system
x: The live session is a complete Aurora desktop that runs from the USB stick and from memory. It works like Ubuntu's “Try Ubuntu”: use it as long as you like; nothing is written to the computer's disks , and everything you change is lost when you shut down. # What is different from an installed system You are logged in automatically as the user aurora , which has no password. sudo works without one. The screen doesn't lock when idle, and the computer doesn't suspend by itself (that would interrupt an installation). The desktop shows Install Aurora OS , and so does the dock. Snapshots, fingerprint and automatic updates are not active. A warning about low disk space is not shown (the live system's “disk” is memory). # Starting the installer Double-click Install Aurora OS on the desktop, or use its icon in the dock. If the installer is already open it comes forward; after you close it, the icon opens it again. See Installing Aurora OS .

d: The installer step by step: language, location, keyboard, disk, user, summary
x: The installer is Calamares with Aurora's look: the steps run across the top as dots that fill in as you go, and there is one Next button. Everything it needs is on the USB stick, so it works offline . Back up your files before installing, above all if you are going to change partitions or install next to another system. # Steps Welcome. Choose the installer's language. It checks the requirements: 20 GB of disk, 2 GB of memory, and the power cable on a laptop. Location. Click your region on the map, or let it be detected. This sets the time zone and the formats for dates, numbers and units. Day and month names always follow the system language; units, numbers and money follow the region. Keyboard. Pick the layout and its variant, and type in the test field. Not sure which one you have? Click Detect… : it asks two or three questions about what is printed on your keys (which letters start the top row, which character is next to L) and selects the layout. Disk. Choose where Aurora goes. What is ready-picked follows your disks: Erase disk when they are all empty, Install alongside when Windows or another system is there, nothing when they hold only data. So Next never wipes another system by mistake: Erase disk : a clean install on the whole disk. Tick Encrypt system for full-disk encryption (LUKS) and choose a passphrase: you'll type it at every start. Install alongside : keeps Windows or another Linux. Click the partition to shrink in the Current bar (Windows' big NTFS one), then drag the divider in the After bar to share the space; the installer proposes half each. Its files stay as they were, and Windows' small EFI partition (100 MB is enough) is shared. Replace a partition : installs onto one existing partition. Manual partitioning : full control. Aurora needs a root partition ( / ) and, on UEFI, an EFI system partition (FAT32, 300 MB or more, mounted on /boot/efi ). The file system is btrfs by default, which gives automatic system snapshots and rollback from the boot menu (see Snapshots and recovery ). ext4 and xfs are available without snapshots. The partition legend shows each partition's name and size. Users. Your full name, user name, password (twice) and the computer's name. Choose Log in automatically to skip the login screen, or leave it off to see it at every start. Summary. Review every choice. Install starts writing to the disk; until then nothing has changed. Installing. A slideshow runs while files are copied, with a progress bar. Once it starts writing to the disk it can't be cancelled (stopping halfway through resizing another system's partition could damage it), so Back, Next and Cancel go away until it finishes. Finish. Tick Restart now and click Done . Remove the USB stick when the computer restarts. # What the installer sets up The boot loader: GRUB, through Debian's signed shim on UEFI (Secure Boot works), or GRUB on the disk on BIOS. Next to Windows, the boot menu lists Windows Boot Manager too (for 5 seconds at every start; Aurora is the default), and Windows' own files in the EFI partition, including its fallback \EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI , are left alone: Aurora lives in \EFI\debian and starts from its own firmware entry. The hardware clock stays in local time, as Windows keeps it, so neither system shows the wrong time after the other. The installed system's boot menu has the USB stick's look: the Aurora logo and a card with Aurora GNU/Linux (started after 5 seconds), Advanced options (the previous kernel and recovery mode), the other systems found (Windows, another Linux), UEFI Firmware Settings and, on btrfs, Aurora OS snapshots . On btrfs: subvolumes @ (system) and @home (your files) with compression, Timeshift, a “Fresh install” snapshot at first boot and the snapshots boot menu. Compressed swap in memory (zram). The firewall (on), automatic security updates (on), and the trixie-backports source for newer kernels when you want them. If the installation fails, the installer offers to save its log. Settings → System Health → Guided Diagnostics can prepare an installation report on the next try (see Troubleshooting ).

d: The Welcome app, and the first things worth doing
x: After the restart you see the login screen (or the desktop, with automatic login), then the Welcome app. It runs once per user and shows: light or dark style; the most useful keyboard shortcuts; where to find apps and settings. Open it again any time from Launchpad ( Welcome ). # Worth doing first Connect to the internet from the Control Center ( Super + S ) → Wi-Fi. Install updates : the system checks a few minutes after login and tells you. Or open App Center → Updates. Set up your fingerprint (Settings → Users), if you have a reader. Add online accounts (Settings → Users → Online Accounts) for mail, calendar and contacts. Pick your look : Settings → Appearance (style, accent color, background) and Settings → Desktop & Dock. Get your tools : Dev Hub for developer tools, Game Hub for games, App Center for everything else.

d: The greeter: logging in, choosing a session, restarting and shutting down
x: The login screen is Aurora Greeter , a GTK 4 app that runs on greetd , the login manager. It shows the Aurora logo and wordmark, the time and date over the current wallpaper, and the users of the computer. # Logging in Click your name, or choose Other… and type a user name. Type your password and press Enter or Log In . A wrong password shows Wrong password. Please try again. The login password also unlocks your keyring, where apps keep saved passwords (Wi-Fi, browsers, Git). # Choosing a session When more than one session is installed, a menu at the bottom of the login screen lists them. Aurora installs two: Session What it is Command Aurora Compatibility Aurora desktop with labwc for systems without working GLES aurora-session labwc Aurora Aurora desktop with animated windows aurora-session wayfire The choice is remembered. See Desktop sessions for the differences. # Restart and shut down Restart and Power Off are in the corner of the login screen. # Automatic login Chosen in the installer, or later in Settings → Users → Log in automatically . greetd then starts your session without asking for the password at boot. The keyring stays locked until an app needs it, and it asks for your password once. # Under the hood greetd runs on virtual terminal 7 ( /etc/greetd/config.toml ). Its default session is /usr/libexec/aurora-greeter-launch , run as the system user _greetd : it reads the system language and keyboard ( /etc/default/locale , /etc/default/keyboard ) and starts the greeter in a locked-down labwc. If the graphical greeter cannot start, greetd's text greeter agreety takes over. After a successful login greetd runs the chosen session's command: aurora-session wayfire or aurora-session labwc (see What happens when you log in ).

d: Aurora (Wayfire) and Aurora Compatibility (labwc): what each is and when to use it
x: Aurora's desktop (top bar, dock, desktop, Spotlight, notifications) is the same in both sessions. What changes is the compositor , the program that draws windows on the screen and handles input. Aurora Aurora Compatibility Compositor Wayfire labwc Window animations Open, close, minimize and restore None (apps keep their own) Snap Layouts and Snap Assist Yes No (snapping with the keyboard works) Zoom (magnifier) shortcuts Super + mouse wheel Super + Alt + 8 , = , − Window menu ( Alt + Space ) No Yes Needs OpenGL ES (a GPU, or software rendering) Nothing special: draws on the processor if needed Use it Normally On old or unusual graphics, or if the Aurora session doesn't start # Choosing the compositor At the login screen, pick the session. Or write wayfire or labwc in ~/.config/aurora/compositor : the Aurora session then uses that compositor. Try Aurora OS (safe graphics) in the boot menu always uses labwc. # Automatic fallback If Wayfire exits with an error within 15 seconds of starting, the session starts labwc instead, and you get a working desktop. The reason is saved in ~/.local/state/aurora/compositor-failure.log and shown in Settings → System Health. On graphics without 3D that expose a render node (VirtualBox or VMware without 3D, virtio-gpu without virgl), Aurora uses labwc from the start, because Mesa cannot draw there for Wayfire. # Configuration Both compositors take their settings from Aurora's Settings app. labwc's configuration is ~/.config/labwc/rc.xml (keyboard shortcuts, input devices, window behavior); Wayfire's, ~/.config/aurora/wayfire.ini , is generated from the same preferences by aurora-wayfire-config each time they change. Edit rc.xml (or use Settings) rather than wayfire.ini .

t: What happens when you log in
d: The session manager: environment, language, keyboard, compositor, shell and autostart, step by step
x: A session is started by /usr/bin/aurora-session , Aurora's session manager. It is a short shell script; this is what it does, in order. # 1. Environment Language. Reads /etc/default/locale , then your own choice from Settings in ~/.config/aurora/locale.conf . If the formats come from another language than the interface (for example English text with Italian formats), day and month names follow the interface language while numbers, units and currency keep the region's. Keyboard. Reads /etc/default/keyboard , then ~/.config/aurora/keyboard.conf , and exports the layout for the compositor ( XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT and friends). Paths and toolkits. Sets the login PATH (including ~/.local/bin ) and the variables that make apps use Wayland: Variable Value in an Aurora session XMODIFIERS @im=fcitx GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx SDL_IM_MODULE=fcitx AURORA_INPUT_METHOD fcitx XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP Aurora:wlroots XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP aurora XDG_SESSION_TYPE wayland MOZ_ENABLE_WAYLAND 1 QT_QPA_PLATFORM wayland;xcb QT_QPA_PLATFORMTHEME gnome SDL_VIDEODRIVER wayland,x11 _JAVA_AWT_WM_NONREPARENTING 1 GTK_USE_PORTAL 1 AURORA_COMPOSITOR labwc AURORA_COMPOSITOR labwc AURORA_COMPOSITOR labwc AURORA_COMPOSITOR labwc Apps started through D-Bus or systemd get the same values: the session hands them to dbus-update-activation-environment when it starts. # 2. Graphics /usr/libexec/aurora-render-env chooses renderers that work on this machine: the GPU when there is one, software rendering in virtual machines without 3D (and the extra settings Hyper-V's display needs). # 3. The compositor Picks Wayfire or labwc (session choice, ~/.config/aurora/compositor , safe graphics, the graphics check above). On first login copies the default labwc configuration to ~/.config/labwc/ , and writes the GTK stylesheet imports for the window style ( aurora-look ). For Wayfire, renders ~/.config/aurora/wayfire.ini and starts it, watching for an early failure (see fallback ). # 4. Startup programs The compositor runs Aurora's startup script ( /usr/share/aurora/labwc/autostart ), which: passes the environment to D-Bus and systemd; creates the standard folders (Desktop, Documents, Downloads…) if missing; applies the display layout saved in Settings ( ~/.config/aurora/displays.sh ); starts Aurora Shell under a watchdog: if the shell ever exits, it starts again, at most five times a minute, until you log out (its log is $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/aurora-shell.log ); starts the administrator password prompt (the polkit agent); runs aurora-autostart , which starts the apps in XDG autostart (yours in ~/.config/autostart and the system's in /etc/xdg/autostart ), honoring OnlyShowIn , NotShowIn , Hidden and TryExec ; manage them in Task Manager → Startup Apps or Settings → Apps; starts aurora-idle (screen off, lock and suspend on inactivity); opens the installer when you chose “Install Aurora OS”, or the Welcome app the first time you log in. # 5. The shell Aurora Shell draws every part of the desktop as Wayland layer surfaces: wallpaper and desktop icons, widgets, top bar, dock, notifications, on-screen indicators, Spotlight, overview and hot corners. It also runs the notification server, the system tray host, clipboard history, Night Light, the dynamic wallpaper, the weather, Storage Sense and screen time. Running aurora-shell again with a command talks to the running shell (see Shell commands ). # Logging out Logging out writes a marker so the watchdog doesn't restart the shell, ends the compositor, and greetd shows the login screen again.

d: When the screen locks, turns off and the computer sleeps, and how to change it
x: # Locking the screen Press Super + L , use the lock button in the Aurora menu or the Control Center, or let it lock when idle. The lock screen ( gtklock in Aurora's style) shows, straight on your current wallpaper, a big clock and the date, and under them your account picture (or your initial), your name and the password field: type the password and press Enter or the arrow. Nothing is drawn around them — the picture darkens at the top and the bottom instead, the way a phone's lock screen does, so the clock and the field read on any wallpaper — and your account picture and the arrow are painted in your accent color, including the accent taken from the background. Under the date it shows what a phone's lock screen shows: a chip with the weather where you are (the last reading, no network call while locked) and one with the battery on a laptop, and, whenever something is playing, a card with the cover, the title and the artist and buttons to go back, pause and skip — they work without unlocking. Each of them is simply absent when there is nothing to say. After 20 seconds without input only the clock stays; move the mouse or press a key to bring the rest back. A wrong password or Caps Lock shows as a small colored note under the field. Its background, and whether it shows your name and picture, are chosen in Settings → Appearance → Lock Screen. Your apps keep running. # On inactivity aurora-idle watches for inactivity with swayidle and follows Settings → Power and Privacy & Security: after the Screen blank delay (Settings → Power): the screen locks, if Automatic screen lock is on; 15 seconds later: the screen turns off; moving the mouse or pressing a key turns it on; after the Automatic Suspend delay (separately on battery and when plugged in): the computer suspends; before suspending, the screen locks. The live session never locks or suspends by itself. # Keep Awake The Keep Awake tile in the Control Center stops screen blanking, locking and automatic suspend until you turn it off: for presentations, long downloads or reading. # Apps that hold off sleep Video players and calls can ask the system not to sleep. When you choose Restart or Shut Down while an app is holding it off, Aurora says which app and offers Restart Anyway or Shut Down Anyway .

d: The power choices, sounds, and what happens to open apps
x: The power choices are at the bottom of the Aurora menu (the logo at the top left) as round buttons, and in the Control Center behind the power button: Sleep Suspends to memory. Open the lid or press a key to wake up; the screen is locked. Restart Closes every app and restarts the computer. Shut Down Closes every app and turns the computer off. Log Out Closes your apps and returns to the login screen. Restart and Shut Down happen right away, after a short goodbye sound; save your work first. If an app is holding them off, Aurora tells you which and offers to go ahead anyway (see Apps that hold off sleep ). Aurora plays a sound when you log in and when you shut down, restart or log out; turn it off in Settings → Sound → Startup and shutdown sounds . The power button and the laptop lid do what Settings → Power says (suspend, shut down, nothing, or ask).

d: The parts of Aurora's desktop and what each is for
x: From top to bottom: Top bar The Aurora menu, the windows of the app in front, the tray, the Assistant (✦), search, status icons and the clock. See Top bar . Desktop Your wallpaper, the files in your Desktop folder and the widgets . Dock Your favorite and open apps, Launchpad and the Trash. See Dock . Over these, when called: Spotlight — tap Super : find and start anything. Launchpad — every app as a grid. Control Center — Super + S : volume, networks, quick toggles. Calendar and notifications — click the clock. Overview — Super + W : every window at once. Snap Layouts — Super + Z : arrange windows side by side. Aurora Assistant — Super + Shift + Space , when Aurora AI is on. The screen itself has rounded corners , like a modern display: four small surfaces paint the corners of every monitor, take no clicks (a window, a desktop icon or a hot corner under them still answers) and follow Settings → Desktop & Dock → Desktop → Rounded screen corners , from 0 px (square) to 24; 14 px to begin with, the same as a window's corners. Everything follows your choices in Settings → Appearance (light or dark, accent color) and Settings → Desktop & Dock (layout, positions, sizes).

d: Every item of the top bar, from left to right
x: By default the bar runs edge to edge. Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar → Style → Floating turns it into rounded islands of frosted glass held off the screen's edge: the menu and windows on the left, the clock in the middle (when it's centered), the status icons on the right. Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar → Blur behind asks the compositor to blur the picture behind the bar, the dock and Spotlight instead of only tinting it. It needs a graphics card and the Aurora session: in the compatibility session it does nothing, and with software rendering — a virtual machine — it is slow or has no effect, so it starts off. Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar → Tint with the accent color gives the bar and the dock a cast of your accent instead of a neutral dark glass — and with Color from the background in Appearance, that accent comes from the picture behind them, so the whole chrome follows the wallpaper through the day. # Left side Aurora menu (logo) Who you are, system-wide actions and the power buttons. See Aurora menu . Windows One button per open window, minimized ones included (dimmer). Click to bring a window forward; click the focused one to minimize it. When an app has several windows, a number shows how many; click it for a list (numbered, to switch) and New Window , Minimize , Close and Quit . Activities Shows file transfers, Dev Hub installs and AI downloads while they run, with their progress. # Right side System monitor (optional) Processor and memory at a glance; its popover adds temperature, download and upload speed and free disk space. Turn it on in Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar. Tray Icons of apps that run in the background (Discord, Slack, Steam, Nextcloud, KDE Connect…). Click for their menu. ✦ Assistant Opens the Aurora Assistant (when Aurora AI is on). Search Opens Spotlight. Status icons Network, volume, Bluetooth, battery (with percentage if chosen), a red dot while recording the screen, and “…”. Click any of them for the Control Center . Scroll over them to change the volume (with the on-screen indicator); middle-click to mute. Show Desktop The thin line at the far right end of the bar, as on Windows: one click hides every window, a second click brings back the ones it hid. Turn it off in Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar. Clock Date and time (24- or 12-hour in Settings → Date & Time; seconds and the clock's position in Settings → Desktop & Dock → Top Bar). Click it for the calendar, weather and notifications . Menus opened with the keyboard close with Esc . The bar can be at the top or the bottom of the screen (Settings → Desktop & Dock).

d: The menu behind the logo: your account, system actions and power
x: Click the Aurora logo at the left of the top bar. Your name and computer Your picture (from Settings → Users), name, the computer's name and the Aurora version. The lock button next to it locks the screen ( Super + L ). About This Computer Settings → About: device name, processor, memory, graphics, disk and versions. System Settings Settings ( Super + I ). App Center Install and update apps. Dev Hub Developer tools in one click. System Health Settings → System Health: problems and their fixes. Task Manager What's running, end tasks, performance ( Ctrl + Shift + Esc ). See Task Manager . Sleep, Restart, Shut Down, Log Out See Shutting down .

d: Volume, brightness, networks and quick toggles, laid out like macOS' Control Center
x: Open it with Super + S or by clicking the status icons in the top bar. Close it with Esc or by clicking outside. # Header The time and date, and the battery charge on laptops (⚡ while charging). # Sliders Volume Drag the knob (the sliders share one card at the top); the level shows in percent. Click the speaker icon on its left to mute. The arrow at its end lists the output devices (speakers, headphones, HDMI, Bluetooth) and, below them, the volume of each app playing sound (see Sound and Volume Mixer ). Microphone When a microphone is present; the arrow chooses the input device. Brightness On laptops and screens that allow it. # Toggles Grouped in three cards: Connections (Wi-Fi, Wired, Bluetooth, Airplane Mode, Mobile Hotspot), Modes (Do Not Disturb, Keep Awake, Power Mode) and Screen (Dark Style, Night Light, Screen Keyboard, Screen Recording). Each shows a round icon, filled with the accent color while on, its name and its state. Click the row to switch it; a small arrow opens a list under the cards. Wi-Fi On or off; the arrow lists networks (click one to connect, a password field appears for protected ones) and links to Network Settings. Wired Shown when a cable is connected; opens Network Settings. Bluetooth On or off; the arrow lists paired devices (click to connect or disconnect), with the battery charge of connected headphones, mice and keyboards that report it. The tile shows the first connected device and its charge. Power Mode Performance, Balanced or Power Saver. Night Light Warmer colors (schedule in Settings → Appearance). Dark Style Switches light and dark; choosing by hand stops the automatic sunset/sunrise switch. Do Not Disturb Silences notification popups (critical ones still show); they stay in the list. Keep Awake No screen blanking, locking or automatic suspend until you turn it off. Airplane Mode Turns Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off together. Mobile Hotspot Shares this computer's internet connection over Wi-Fi, like a phone's hotspot (on computers with Wi-Fi). The arrow shows the network's name (the computer's name followed by “Aurora”) and its password, made up the first time and kept (click it to copy), and, while on, a QR code: point a phone's camera at it to join. Change the name or password with gsettings set org.aurora.desktop hotspot-name / hotspot-password . Screen Keyboard Shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (for touch screens and tablets). It types into the app you were using without taking its focus: ⇧ for a capital (twice for Caps), ?123 and =\< for numbers and symbols, Ctrl for shortcuts (Ctrl, then C), arrows, and ✕ to hide it. Its look is chosen in Settings → Accessibility → Keyboard theme (ten themes). Also aurora-shell osk show|hide|toggle . Screen Recording Starts recording the screen (after the panel closes) or stops it; the arrow chooses the whole screen or an area, and whether the computer's sound is recorded. Recordings go to ~/Videos/Screencasts . # Media When something is playing (a browser, Spotify, Celluloid…), its title, artist and previous / play-pause / next. # Bottom row Battery time, then Screenshot (of an area), Settings , Lock and the power menu (Suspend, Restart, Power Off, Log Out).

d: The clock's popover: calendar, weather, notification history and Do Not Disturb
x: Click the clock in the top bar. # Calendar Today's full date and a month calendar (arrows change month and year). Open Calendar opens GNOME Calendar with your events. # Weather The temperature, the sky and the next hours, for: the city chosen in the Weather app, if any; otherwise Weather's automatic location (found through GeoClue, rounded to about 10 km); otherwise the main city of your time zone. Choosing a city in Weather updates it at once. Units follow Weather's setting, else your region. Data comes from Open-Meteo (no account, only that approximate position is sent) and is kept for 30 minutes. Click the weather to open the Weather app. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy & Security. # Notifications New notifications pop up at the top right for a few seconds; critical ones stay. Click one to open the app that sent it; buttons on it run its actions. The popover keeps the history: Clear empties it, Do Not Disturb silences the popups. When a notification contains a one-time code (“Your verification code is 482913”), it gets a Copy 482913 button. Per-app choices (mute an app's notifications) are in Settings → Notifications. # Warnings Aurora sends by itself Updates ready, and a restart needed to finish them; the battery low (10%) and critically low (5%), and Battery Saver turning on; a Bluetooth device low on battery : headphones, a mouse or a keyboard at 15% or less (once, until it has been charged again); a disk nearly full, a drive plugged in. # Automatic Do Not Disturb Like Windows' Focus Assist, Do Not Disturb can turn on by itself (Settings → Notifications → Automatic Do Not Disturb): On a schedule , from and to an hour you choose (22:00–07:00 by default; off until you turn it on); While an app is fullscreen : games, videos and presentations (on by default); While sharing or recording the screen (on by default). The gap replaces the hairline before the Trash; the one between pinned and open apps stays. A pill with nothing in it (the Trash turned off) isn't drawn. Always Hidden until the pointer reaches the edge, whatever is on screen. # Settings Settings → Desktop & Dock: position (bottom, left or right), the style above, icon size, magnification when pointing, when it gets out of the way, whether apps that are only open appear, and which apps are pinned. d: Light and dark, accent colors, backgrounds, picture of the day, icons, fonts and Night Light
x: Settings → Appearance. # Background On top, a preview of your desktop. Personalize your background chooses what fills it: Dynamic (follows the sun) The Aurora landscape changes through the day (dawn, day, dusk, night) with the sun where you are, and crossfades between them. Series picks which of the three included sets of pictures it uses: Starfall (the default, with the Milky Way at night), Veil (misty valleys) or Horizon (calm, simple ridges). Each of the twelve pictures can also be chosen on its own as a Picture, or shown in a slideshow. Picture Recent images shows the pictures used lately; Browse Photos… picks any image (a copy goes to ~/.local/share/backgrounds ); All Wallpapers… opens a searchable gallery of every wallpaper, which only draws the thumbnails in view, so it stays quick with thousands of pictures. Picture of the day A new background every day from Bing , NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day or Wikimedia Commons' Picture of the Day , with its title and credit under the preview. Aurora asks the service for today's picture once a day and keeps the last week in ~/.local/share/aurora/daily ; nothing else is sent. Slideshow Pictures from a folder of your choice (its subfolders too), or the included ones, changing every 15 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours or 24 hours, in order or shuffled. Hidden folders are skipped; in a very large folder only the first 20,000 entries are looked at, and pictures added later join within 10 minutes. Solid color One of twelve colors, or any color with the color button. Wallpapers are looked for in /usr/share/backgrounds , ~/.local/share/backgrounds and ~/Pictures/Wallpapers . The lock screen shows the picture on screen, unless you choose otherwise in Lock Screen , under Background: Same as the desktop , The desktop's, blurred (a soft, darker copy, made once per picture) or A picture of its own; and Show my name and picture , which can be turned off so the lock screen shows only the time, the date and the password field. The login screen, which comes before any account's settings, shows the Starfall series at the time of day. # Style Color scheme : Light, Dark or Auto (dark from sunset to sunrise where you are). It changes the apps and the desktop widgets; the desktop itself — the top bar, the dock, Spotlight, Launchpad, the Control Center, notifications — stays dark glass over your wallpaper in both, as one piece. Density : Comfortable or Compact . Compact shortens the top bar and tightens the menus, the Control Center, notifications, Spotlight and the dock's row — the same desktop with less room around everything, for a small screen or for fitting more on one. Accent color : nine colors, used by buttons, selections, switches, widgets and the Control Center. Color from the background : instead of one of the nine, Aurora takes the most vivid color of the picture on screen and uses it everywhere. The picture is read small and its colors gathered by hue; the one that wins is pulled into a range that still reads under white text, so a washed-out or very dark picture never gives an unusable accent, and a picture with no color at all (a grey photograph) leaves your chosen accent alone. With the dynamic background on it follows the sky: blue through the day, rose at dusk. Aurora's own apps (Files, Settings, Task Manager, Dev Hub…) have surfaces with a faint violet tint, in both styles, and switch with the style at once; other apps keep their own colors. Icons : Aurora (light and dark variants), Papirus, or any installed icon theme. Pointer and its size. Animations (all interface animations: menus, the Control Center and the calendar growing in; a notification sliding in from the corner; the volume and brightness indicators rising; a dock icon bouncing while its app starts, and giving under a click; tiles and window cards lifting under the pointer) and Window animations (opening, closing, minimizing windows; files floating in when a folder opens; the menus of apps). With them off, everything appears and disappears at once. libadwaita, GTK 3, GTK 4 and Qt apps all follow the style and accent color. # Fonts Interface, document and monospace fonts and sizes, scaling, anti-aliasing and hinting. Aurora uses Inter for the interface, JetBrains Mono for code, and Noto for every script. # Night Light Warmer colors in the evening: from sunset to sunrise, on your own schedule, or all the time; choose the warmth. It changes the screen's color tables, which the graphics driver has to allow: virtual machines and a few drivers don't. Then Aurora says so with a notification and on the Night Light settings, instead of silently doing nothing; on a computer, installing the graphics driver (Settings → Updates → Additional Drivers) usually fixes it.

d: One-click installers for editors, languages, cloud tools, databases, containers and more, and project workspaces
x: Dev Hub installs developer tools from their official sources, so they are always current. Each install runs in a progress window with an embedded terminal: it shows every command, keeps the log visible if something fails, and asks for the administrator password there when needed. Any other copy of the same repository — left by the vendor's own package, by an earlier attempt, or by a how-to followed by hand — is moved aside with a .aurora-disabled suffix and named in the log. d: Writing a disk image to a USB stick, and checking that it arrived
h: Giving a stick its life back
x: USB Stick Writer (Launchpad, or right-click an image in Files → Open With ) puts a disk image on a USB stick — an Aurora ISO to install from, or any other system's. Choose the image : an .iso or .img . Compressed downloads work as they are ( .gz , .xz , .bz2 , .zst , and a .zip holding a single image): they are unpacked while they are written, so there is no need to unpack a five-gigabyte download first. Choose the stick. Only removable and USB disks are listed, and the disk this system is running from is never among them — nor, on a live session, the stick you booted from. A disk that is mounted says where, and is unmounted for you. Erase and Write. The dialog names the stick, its size and the image; everything on the stick is replaced. # Checking the download first Check the download compares the file with its SHA-256 — the long line of letters and numbers a download page gives you. If the download came with one beside it ( aurora-os-0.1-amd64.iso.sha256 , or a SHA256SUMS naming it), it is filled in for you; otherwise paste it from the page. Check reads the file through and says whether it matches. Worth doing before writing: a half-finished download makes an installer that fails in the middle, and the check is the only way to tell one from a good one by looking. # Options Check the stick afterwards On by default. Reads the stick back when the write is done and compares it with the image, byte for byte. Worth the extra minute: a stick that quietly drops writes is the usual reason a freshly made installer won't boot, and a counterfeit stick that claims more space than it has is caught here rather than halfway through an installation. Eject when finished On by default. Flushes the stick and powers it down, so it can be pulled out as soon as the window says so. Both are remembered for next time. # Giving a stick its life back A stick that has carried an installer is no use for files: it holds a read-only image, and Windows offers to format it. The menu's Erase the Stick… makes it one empty disk again, with a name you choose and a format: exFAT (the default — Windows and macOS read it too, and it holds files larger than 4 GB), FAT32 (what the oldest things read) or Ext4 (Linux only, with permissions). Writing asks for your password, because overwriting a disk needs it. The checks above are made again by the part that runs with those privileges ( /usr/libexec/aurora-usb-write ), so a mistake or a misbehaving program cannot talk it into writing over the system's own disk.

x: On a btrfs installation (the installer's default) Aurora keeps snapshots of the system: Fresh install , taken at the first boot; one before every update or package installation (the last 10); daily (the last 5) and weekly (the last 3). They cover the system, not your files in Home: rolling back never loses your documents. # If an update breaks something Restart. In the boot menu (shown for 5 seconds at every start) choose Aurora OS snapshots , then the snapshot from before the update: each reads what it is and when, like Before: apt | 2026-10-07 09:12:40 . Inside, pick Aurora OS, Linux … (the kernel versions that snapshot has). Aurora starts as it was then (read-only for the system). Check that everything works. Open Timeshift (Settings → Software Updates → Open Timeshift), select the same snapshot and click Restore . Restart once more: the rollback is permanent. # Managing snapshots Settings → Software Updates → Take a Snapshot Now , or turn the automatic ones off ( Snapshot before every update ). d: Running Aurora in QEMU, GNOME Boxes, virt-manager, VirtualBox and VMware
h: On a server, watched from another computer
x: Aurora runs well in a virtual machine. Give it 4 GB of memory (8 GB for AI models), 2 or more processors and a 40 GB disk . Guest tools for QEMU/KVM (agent, SPICE), VirtualBox, VMware and Hyper-V are included. # Graphics in a VM With 3D acceleration (virtio-gpu with virgl, VirtualBox or VMware with 3D on) the Aurora session uses it. Without it, Wayfire draws on the processor, or Aurora uses the Compatibility session where Wayfire can't run (see Desktop sessions ). # GNOME Boxes and virt-manager Open the ISO, choose Debian 13 as the operating system, 4 GB of memory and 2 or more processors. virt-manager: enable UEFI (OVMF) if you want it. # QEMU from a terminal sudo apt install qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils ovmf # Debian/Ubuntu qemu-img create -f qcow2 aurora.qcow2 40G qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -machine q35 -cpu host -smp 4 -m 4G \ -cdrom aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso -boot d \ -drive file=aurora.qcow2,if=virtio \ -device virtio-vga-gl -display gtk,gl=on \ -device intel-hda -device hda-duplex \ -nic user,model=virtio-net-pci -usb -device usb-tablet -device virtio-vga-gl -display gtk,gl=on gives the VM 3D acceleration. Without it (for example over SSH) use -vga std -display gtk . Add -drive if=pflash,format=raw,readonly=on,file=/usr/share/OVMF/OVMF_CODE_4M.fd to boot with UEFI; keep the same firmware for later boots. After installing, start again without -cdrom and -boot d . From Aurora's source tree, build/run-qemu.sh does this with options ( --uefi , --disk FILE , --software , --spice PORT , --vnc N ). # On a server, watched from another computer # on the server build/run-qemu.sh --uefi --disk aurora.qcow2 --spice 5930 aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso # on your computer ssh -L 5930:127.0.0.1:5930 user@server remote-viewer spice://127.0.0.1:5930 # Windows with WSL 2 WSL 2 supports nested virtualization, so the QEMU commands work in Ubuntu on WSL: check that /dev/kvm exists, install QEMU, add yourself to the kvm group ( sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER , then wsl --shutdown ), and start with --software . # VirtualBox and VMware Create a Debian 64-bit VM, enable EFI for UEFI, give it 128 MB of video memory and turn 3D acceleration on if available. The guest tools are already in Aurora.

x: Hyper-V is in Windows 10 and 11 Pro, Enterprise and Education. Hyper-V never gives a Linux VM your graphics card for its screen: the desktop is drawn by Hyper-V's virtual display, in software. Options: -Name , -MemoryGB , -Processors , -DiskGB , -Folder , -Switch , -Width , -Height , -NoStart , -Recreate . # Install Install as on a PC ( Installing Aurora OS ). After the restart the VM starts from its disk; remove the ISO from the DVD drive in the VM's settings when you no longer need it. # If the installed system doesn't start It shows “Start PXE over IPv4” The network is before the disk in the boot order: Set-VMFirmware -VMName Aurora -BootOrder (Get-VMDvdDrive -VMName Aurora), (Get-VMHardDiskDrive -VMName Aurora), (Get-VMNetworkAdapter -VMName Aurora) The firmware can't read the disk On some hosts the VM's firmware reads the virtual disk only through a checkpoint. d: Short answers to common questions
x: Is Aurora OS free? Yes: free to use, share and change, under the GPL 3.0 or later. It has no ads, no telemetry and needs no account. Can I install Windows programs? Many: Game Hub sets up Bottles and Wine for Windows apps, and Steam's Proton for games. Look for a Linux version or a web version first (App Center, Flathub). Can I use Android apps? Game Hub installs Waydroid, which runs Android apps in a window. Does it have a Microsoft Office equivalent? LibreOffice (Writer, Calc, Impress) opens and saves Office files. Microsoft 365 works in the browser. Where are my files? In your home folder, /home/YOUR-NAME : Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Music, Pictures, Videos. How do I install something that's not in App Center? A .deb file: double-click it, or sudo apt install ./file.deb . An AppImage: make it executable in Properties and open it. Dev Hub covers most developer tools. How do I become administrator in a terminal? Put sudo before the command; it asks your password (or your finger). Can I keep Windows? Yes: Install alongside in the installer; the boot menu then lets you choose at every start. Why is the Windows drive read-only? Windows didn't shut down completely, so Linux must not write to its drive: Fast Startup (on by default in Windows 10 and 11) and hibernation leave it in use, and so does the disk check Windows runs once after Aurora is installed next to it. Files then opens it read-only and says so; your files are all there to copy. To change files on it, start Windows and choose Restart (not Shut down) back into Aurora, or turn Fast Startup off in Windows (Control Panel → Power Options → Choose what the power buttons do). Opening it asks for your password once. Why does the time differ from Windows after switching? Windows keeps the hardware clock in local time, Linux in UTC. When the installer finds Windows it sets Aurora to local time too, so both agree. If Windows was added later, run sudo timedatectl set-local-rtc 1 in Aurora. How do I change the language later? Settings → Language & Region, then log out and in. Is my data sent anywhere? Only what's listed in Security and privacy → What goes online by itself .

d: Words used in this documentation
x: Compositor The program that draws windows on the screen and passes them input: Wayfire or labwc in Aurora. Wayland The modern way Linux apps show windows. Older X11 apps run through Xwayland. Shell Aurora Shell: the top bar, dock, desktop, Spotlight, notifications and widgets. (Also: the command interpreter in a terminal, bash.) Layer surface A part of the desktop that isn't a window (bar, dock, wallpaper), drawn above or below windows. Greeter The login screen. Session Everything that runs from login to logout. Snapshot An instant copy of the system on btrfs, to go back to after a bad update. Flatpak A format for sandboxed apps that work on any distribution; Flathub is its main store. Portal The way sandboxed apps ask for files, the camera or the screen. polkit The system that asks for the administrator password for privileged actions. Live session Aurora running from the USB stick without installing.

d: Requirements, make targets, build stages and developing the desktop without an ISO
x: # Requirements A Linux computer with Docker (or Podman), about 25 GB of free disk space and a network connection. Building takes 20–60 minutes the first time. # Build git clone https://github.com/padovanl/auroraOS cd auroraOS make iso # out/aurora-os-VERSION-amd64.iso and its .sha256 # Make targets Target What it does make iso Builds the ISO in a container, stage by stage. make run , make run-uefi Boots the ISO in QEMU (BIOS or UEFI). make debs , make repo Builds Aurora's packages and the signed apt repository. make site Rebuilds the website from the README and docs/_src . make manual Rebuilds this documentation from docs/_manual . make -C desktop pot Regenerates the translation template. make test and friends See Testing . # Stages Stage What it does 10-bootstrap debootstrap creates a minimal Debian trixie. 20-packages Installs the package lists in config/packages/ , translations and locales. 25-extras Third-party packages verified by checksum. 30-system Copies overlay/ , writes Aurora's identity. 35-defaults Firewall, automatic updates, Flathub, Docker, shell setup. 40-desktop Builds and installs aurora-desktop and aurora-artwork . 50-branding Boot splash, GRUB theme, installer branding. 70-pool Offline packages for the installer. 80-finalize initramfs, cleanup. 90-iso SquashFS, the GRUB menu, a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO. # Changing the desktop without rebuilding The desktop is Python: run it from a checkout with AURORA_LIBDIR=$PWD/desktop desktop/bin/aurora-files , or start a headless development session with the tools in desktop/dev/ . In a running VM, tests/interact/serve.py and do.py push the checkout's code and drive the desktop. Every app with a libadwaita window imports aurora.plaintext first: rows ( Adw.ActionRow , ComboRow , SwitchRow …) and toasts then show their title and subtitle as plain text, so names with & or < appear as they are. d: Adding or fixing translations of Aurora's own apps
x: Strings are marked with gettext ( _("…") ) in the domain aurora . Regenerate the template: make -C desktop pot . It also takes the apps' names and descriptions from desktop/data/applications/*.desktop ; make install writes them back with every language ( Name[it]=File ), so Launchpad and the dock show them translated. A language needs its line in desktop/po/LINGUAS . Translations are kept as JSON in desktop/po/sources/LANG.json : English text → translation; plurals as a list with one form per plural category. Build the .po file: tools/po-from-json.py LANG . It rejects a translation whose {placeholders} differ from the English, so a typo can't break the app. To add a language to the system, add a line to config/locales.list .
